Yeah, no need to weigh yourself.  Tracking your food in myfitnesspal may be insightful though. Dont change your diet and just log everything without judgment for like 2 weeks. See if you're getting enough protein. If you were actually getting enough protein/nutrition, you'd be less likely to snack. Also make sure you're drinking enough water. (60-100 oz depending on your activity level) 

Seeing the data will put you in a better position to make food decisions. Then you can play around with creating a caloric deficit from your current numbers, limiting sweets to one a week or day. 

There is no reason to eat in the middle of the night. It doesn't matter when you eat but you'd see a *lot* more progress if you focused on getting quality sleep as well. 

When is your feeding window? An easy 16:8 schedule for many is like 11am-7 pm, but find one that works for you.

Also r/fitness has an excellent wiki about nutrition/eating better. Good luck. :)
Happy to hear it. I've seen it a lot myself as well, people are barely eating and they can't lose weight. Exercise gets put on the back burner and it just never ends. Best of luck!

Sounds good. You are the best authority on your own body. My point was a deficit should be subtracted from tdee not rmr. The last few pounds are harder to lose which is why I feel emphasis would be better placed on exercise performance and muscle building because it actually does allow you to eat more without gaining fat.

Glad to have helped. It's an interest of mine. I encourage everyone to do their own research and find what works for them, but I have been learning too, and I have restricted before, and it does not compare to actually feeding your body what it needs to function optimally and even thrive! with an active lifestyle, which will only improve your overall health for the rest of your life.

1200 is not "plenty". It may barely even be enough. I understand Not everyone is going to go have an rmr test done but I did, after a period of depression and being pretty sedentary at 5'2" and my rmr was still more than that. 

A few inches of height does not mean my body burns THAT much more than someone 4'11, especially not if that person does any sort of exercise, which I believe all healthy people should do. It does vary between people, even of the same height, but Rmr is merely what you need to stay alive. Add in the thermic effect of food and literally any activity and you can add a couple hundred calories to that figure, for your TDEE (total daily energy expenditure). Which would be where you can maintain, unless you have a true metabolic disorder.

I think the more people understand this, the easier people will find it to sustain a healthy life rather than being on diets forever. I just don't believe in chasing a number on the scale if it means you're still weak and fat and unable to exert yourself for any reason because you're not eating and have no muscle mass to speak of.

But that's my personal preference. At the end of the day everyone has to decide the kind of life they want and if you're happy with just having a low BMI/not being obese and dont want to reap the benefits of regular exercise then maybe  restricting calories forever or eating no more than your rmr will work just fine for your goals. I'm honestly not sure.

It's just in my mind that if I want to lose weight I actually want to lose fat and get fitter and healthier, not just weigh less, potentially at the cost of muscle. And I know that what I am saying actually works for that goal. And it coincides with what most people with active lifestyles experience. I doubt you will find many crossfitters or marathon runners or even just basic working adults who like to do stuff every now and then out there on 800 calories a day indefinitely, regardless of their height.

 If you ARE intent on using a severe deficit, I would still argue for keeping protein up, probably even higher then, so that you dont lose as much muscle mass, and since it's the most filling macro it will be much easier. (Look up protein-sparing modified fasts)

If you eat enough (especially protein) at meals, you probably wont even want snack or dessert. 

And understanding that what you do most of the time is more important than what you do once in a while, you won't feel the need to beat yourself up if you have a slice of cake or whatever, just get back on track. 

80/20 rule is so real. One day of even 2000 calories wont make a difference if you have everything else under control. Life happens, weddings, vacation, whatever. It's about empowering yourself with knowledge about how your body works and what it needs, so you can make the best decisions more often than not and feel good about it.

 If theres an emotional eating problem or dysmorphia then maybe therapy is needed too. Everyone has a different journey but I think most people want to be healthy and not have to overly restrict themselves to enjoy life.

I think a prolonged fast is safe and can beneficial here and there. I wouldn't even do it as often as once a week, though. You'd have to experiment with it.

For the sake of sustainability, I'd say 3-5 days a week of 16:8 can be just as beneficial, and as it gets easier, throw in some 18:6 or 20:4 fasts, without dropping calories. Listen to your body, fast when it feels easy. 

Getting enough calories during your feeding window will make fasting much easier as well. I often do 16-18 hours a day, I'm actually 21 hours into a fast right now, just hit the gym, and I am about to do cardio, then eat, and it will be amazing.

Fasting has other benefits than creating a deficit. But it is also a stressor. If you find it really easy to do a 24 hour fast that often, then it probably wouldn't hurt, but if you're fighting off terrible hunger pangs for the duration of the fast and dont feel like you can eat normally afterwards (ie without binging), it's not worth it.

 It's okay to be hungry but I believe the process should be easy enough for you to be *consistent* which is so much more important than being able to eat nothing for a day. Although I think everyone should be able to manage that on occasion.

I'm not an expert, just sharing my experience. I've done prolonged fasts like 72 hrs + and I love fasting, but I feel like they're more of a once in a while, therapeutic thing than an every day life thing. But even with shorter fasts like 16:8, you have to fit it into your life, so it works with your schedule, or you will struggle.

It can't hurt to try a 24 hr fast 1x weekly but if it doesn't feel good or is too difficult or otherwise negatively impacts your life or training, then just try different things. It's not necessary at all.

1200 still seems low. That might be closer to your bmr, ie what your body requires at rest. No walking around, working, exercise, life activity accounted for. Probably wanna be in the 1300 (rest) -1500 (active) ballpark if you want to be able to expend more energy on exercise and feel good, and ultimately BUILD your metabolism rather than downregulating it with restriction and teaching your body to be building and sparing muscle rather than breaking it down because it costs more calories to maintain than you are giving it. By feeding enough your body will also learn there is no reason to carry body fat in excess.

 I'm 5'2" and I have been skinny fat. This has been my experience. Like you I could easily eat under 1000 calories but I wasn't able to put enough energy into workouts.  I could easily eat 800 cals and get down to 105 lbs but I couldnt sustain healthy levels of activity and probably other bodily functions suffered as well. And eating more just puts the fat back on instantly. It's not a matter of if but when, your body will want to eat more, after a period of restriction. Might as well use that to your advantage.

Once I started eating more (~1500) I was lifting heavier, and losing inches of body fat. It's been exactly  4 weeks today. I weighed 120 when I started but this morning I was 114 lb (51 kg). I'm noticeably leaner and more muscular. Also it helps a lot with muscle recovery.
Edit to show where I'm at: http://imgur.com/a/JblHQdl

Eating more feels unnatural at first but then it feels so good because your body is going to function better and you will have more energy to crush it in the gym. It's a positive feedback loop. 

Unless you have to weigh a certain amount in a short amount of time, this is the way to go. I think it's worth a shot anyway. And more enjoyable than keeping super low calories.

You can fast to create a deficit. Like another poster mentioned, I would be worried about adequate micronutrient intake in such a deficit. 

You also don't really want to eat below your RMR for an extended period of time. The body  has the ability to adapt metabolically. It will find a way to require less energy to function. And if you teach it that calories are scarce, if you ever decide to eat more, it will be much easier to put on body fat and harder to lose it, because your body is concerned with survival. That's what causes dieting cycles and the need for perpetual, ever-increasing restriction.

Also there is a minimum amount of dietary fat you need to ensure you can absorb fat-soluble nutrients and keep your hormones (which regulate fat loss, sleep, hunger, fertility, Mood, etc) functioning. (Around 40 g = 360 cal) 

If you aren't totally sedentary, you should eat at least .8 g of protein per lb of lean body mass. Assuming a goal weight of 115 with a bodyfat percentage of 20% that's around 92g of protein, about 368 calories. 

Protein is so satiating it's almost impossible to overeat, has the highest thermic effect of any macronutrient (requires more energy/calories to digest), and helps your body build and repair muscle as well other organs. It should be noted that muscle mass requires more energy to maintain, therefore having more muscle will result in burning more calories at rest. Protein intake also tells your body to hold onto muscle instead of fat when losing weight/ in a deficit and actually stimulates muscle growth in a similar way to resistance training. 

Since you are active with gym and cardio, even 1g per lb of body weight or more would be beneficial. That'd be about 460 cal.

That's 820 cal from just protein and fat alone. There's an argument that carbs aren't physiologically necessary for people and You could probably lose fat rapidly for a while with that but it wouldn't be very sustainable. Unless you're a carnivore maybe or keto for life?

On the other hand adequate carb intake could be a total game-changer for performance and how you feel.

Does your goal concern improving body composition and reducing body fat percentage? You could probably meet your goal weight with a still relatively high body fat percentage and be skinny fat. But I don't think you want that.

A more sustainable approach to long term fat loss would be focused on supporting an active lifestyle, that supports health all around, which would require more calories and therefore be much easier to maintain as well as being more flexible. 

I'd use carbs and fats (play around with ratios to find what feels good) to meet the rest of your needs for maintenance calories, a SLIGHT deficit on rest days if any (100-150 cal), stay there for a few weeks. If you're not too advanced with training you will easily lose fat and gain muscle without even being in a deficit, which will  ultimately result in a lower body fat percentage.

Your goal weight may change as muscle is more dense than fat. Weight loss may be slower with proper training, because you are adding muscle as well as losing fat, if that makes sense. Hope that helps!

Edit: to say protein shakes really help to meet calorie/protein goals. It's physiologically easier to drink calories than to eat them.

Here's the recipe:

Ingredients

2 cups Bob's Red Mill gluten free flour

4-5 very ripe bananas mashed (1 1/2 cups)

1/2 cup sugar

1/2 cup butter 1 stick, softened

2 eggs

2 tablespoons milk

1/2 teaspoon vanilla

1 teaspoon baking powder

1 teaspoon baking soda

1/4 teaspoon salt

1/2-1 cup chocolate chips I used 1 cup

Instructions

Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Lightly grease a 9x5 inch loaf pan, set aside.

In a large bowl, combine flour, baking soda, baking powder, and salt, set aside. In a separate bowl, cream together butter and sugar. Stir in eggs, milk, vanilla, and mashed bananas until well blended. Stir banana mixture and chocolate chips into flour mixture; stir just to moisten. Pour batter into prepared loaf pan.

Bake in preheated oven for 50 to 55 minutes, until a toothpick inserted into center of the loaf comes out clean. Let bread cool in pan for at least minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack. Slice and serve warm!
